extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media industry professionals, and readers interested in media business news
extracted.subtask_description: A short news report summarizing an investigation (by Futurism) that found phrasing similarities in CNET's AI-generated stories to previously published articles and discussing expert reaction. The page is aimed at informing readers about alleged plagiarism and its implications for journalism ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: A Futurism investigation found extensive evidence that the CNET’s artificial intelligence-produced stories show phrasing similarities to articles previously published elsewhere, without giving credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states the bot 'directly plagiarized the work of Red Ventures competitors, as well as human writers at Bankrate and even CNET itself.' It reports an expert (Jeff Schatten) reviewed numerous examples provided and found they 'clearly' rose to the level of plagiarism. Use repeated, close phrasing similarities and lack of attribution as indicators when assessing AI-generated pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution / crediting sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When material (including phrasing) from other publications is used, the original sources must be credited; failure to do so is presented as a core element of plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes 'without giving credit' as central to the allegation. For evaluating journalistic work—human- or AI-produced—check whether passages mirror prior coverage and whether appropriate attribution or citation is provided. Lack of attribution to competitors or previously published pieces is treated as a substantive ethical breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert review and pattern-based determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments of plagiarism rely on review of multiple examples and expert judgment about whether similarities constitute copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff Schatten 'reviewed numerous examples of the bot’s apparent cribbing' and concluded the examples 'clearly' rose to plagiarism. This implies a standard of showing a pattern across pieces and having knowledgeable reviewers evaluate the degree and nature of similarity rather than relying on a single surface match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences illustrated by academic analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparable behavior (submitting work with repeated un-attributed similarities) would trigger formal disciplinary processes and severe sanctions in academic contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asked what would happen if a student turned in an essay with similar un-attributed similarities, Schatten said: 'They would be sent to the student-run ethics council and given the repeated nature of the behavior would almost certainly be expelled from the university.' The article uses this analogy to underline seriousness and possible reputational/disciplinary consequences in journalism.
